newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain spokesman denies threatening media executive.
newsitem.headline: Spain spokesman denies threatening media executive.

text.p: Spain's chief government spokesman denied on Monday that he had threatened a media executive with jail -- an accusation that had last week strained already tense relations among the main political parties.

"I never threatened Mr Asensio with jail and the proof given by my supposed adversaries is words that another person, it seems, never said," the spokesman, Miguel Angel Rodriguez, told a congressional committee in a voluntary appearance.
He added that if such threats were made, they did not come from his office in Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's residence.

Rodriguez, who was alleged to have warned Antena 3 chairman Antonio Asensio that he could end up in prison over disputed soccer rights, said the charges were part of a plot by the leading opposition Socialist party to discredit him.
Socialist party leader and former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez accused the year-old conservative government of abusing the freedom of the press in statements he made last month in Mexico.

Asensio later said before Congress that he had received a threatening phone call from the government spokesman because he had abandoned a government-favoured digital television project for a rival group.
On Monday, after Rodriguez' appearance, Antena 3 issued a statement again defending Asensio and criticising the government spokesman.

"In the present media war over the Digital Platforms, Mr Rodriguez has not remained neutral as he asserted before Parliament, but has played openly in favour of some companies and against others," the statement said.

The controversy brought the year-old Popular Party government to near-crisis last week when its key parliamentary allies warned that they too were worried about the pressure Rodriguez was alleged to have exerted on Asensio and that their support was far from guaranteed.
The Socialists have called for a special parliamentary committee to investigate "abuses of power" with the media.

In the Constitution Committee on Monday, a spokesman for Spain's third largest party, the United Left, said Rodriguez should resign because he had got the government embroiled in what was essentially a dispute among competing media interests.

"You should change office because as a specialist in communication you don't appear to carry out this task well," United Left spokesman Felipe Alcaraz said, adding that the dispute made it appear that the media better represented citizens than the politicians.
"These days the business powers live and are seen in the halls of Congress in a way that until now has never happened."
